questions.q: The rate of a reaction is increased by a catalyst because the catalyst:
questions.solution:
A catalyst offers a **different mechanism with a lower $E_{a}$**, so a far larger fraction of collisions is energetic enough to succeed.

It does **not** move the equilibrium position — it lowers the barrier equally in both directions, so equilibrium is reached **sooner** but at the same place.
options: increases the energy of the molecules
provides an alternative route of lower activation energy

questions.q: For a first order reaction, the half-life:
questions.solution:
A **constant** half-life is the signature of a first order reaction — and the quickest way to identify one from a concentration-time graph.

For zero order the half-life **halves** each time; for second order it **doubles**.

questions.q: For $\text{N}_{2} + 3\text{H}_{2} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_{3}$ ($\Delta H$ negative), the yield of ammonia is increased by:
questions.solution:
**Low temperature** favours the exothermic forward reaction; **high pressure** favours the side with fewer gas molecules (2 against 4).

But a low temperature makes the reaction impossibly slow, which is why the Haber process uses a **compromise** at $450$°C with an iron catalyst.

questions.q: $K_{c}$ is affected by a change in:
questions.solution:
**Only temperature** changes $K_{c}$.

Changing concentration or pressure shifts the **position** of equilibrium, but the system moves to restore the same value of $K_{c}$. A catalyst changes neither.

**Both reactions continue**, at equal rates, so the concentrations stay constant — which is why it is called **dynamic**.

Adding a radioactively labelled reactant proves it: the label soon appears in the products even though nothing measurable has changed.
options: the forward and reverse rates are equal

questions.q: A rate constant has units mol$^{-1}$dm$^{3}$s$^{-1}$. Find the order of the reaction.
questions.solution:
Units of $k$ are $\left(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\right)^{1-n}\text{s}^{-1}$.

Matching $\text{mol}^{-1}\text{dm}^{3}$ gives $1 - n = -1$, so $n = \mathbf{2}$.

questions.q: For rate $= k[A][B]^{2}$, by what factor does the rate change if $[B]$ is doubled?
A first order reaction has $k = 0.0347$ s$^{-1}$. Find its half-life, in s.
For $\text{A} \rightleftharpoons \text{B}$ at equilibrium, $[\text{A}] = 0.2$ and $[\text{B}] = 0.8$ mol dm$^{-3}$. Find $K_{c}$.
questions.solution:
$K_{c} = \dfrac{[\text{B}]}{[\text{A}]} = \dfrac{0.8}{0.2} = \mathbf{4}$.

A value above 1 means the products are favoured.

questions.q: Doubling $[A]$ quadruples the rate. Find the order with respect to $A$.
Explain how the order of a reaction is determined from initial rate data, and deduce the rate equation from: doubling $[A]$ doubles the rate; doubling $[B]$ leaves the rate unchanged.
questions.solution:
**The method of initial rates.** Change **one** concentration at a time, keeping the others fixed, and see how the initial rate responds.

The **initial** rate is used because at that moment the concentrations are known exactly, before any product has built up to complicate matters.

**Interpreting the result for a single reactant:**

• Doubling the concentration **doubles** the rate — **first** order ($2^{1} = 2$).

• Doubling **quadruples** it — **second** order ($2^{2} = 4$).

• Doubling leaves it **unchanged** — **zero** order ($2^{0} = 1$).

**Applying this.**

Doubling $[A]$ doubles the rate: **first order in A**.

Doubling $[B]$ changes nothing: **zero order in B**.

$\mathbf{\text{rate} = k[A]}$, and the overall order is **1**.

**What zero order in B tells you about the mechanism.** $B$ does not appear in the **rate-determining step** — the slowest step of the mechanism.

Only species involved up to and including that step appear in the rate equation, whatever the balanced equation says.

**This is why the rate equation cannot be written from the stoichiometry.** It must be found experimentally, and when it disagrees with the balanced equation, that disagreement is itself evidence about the mechanism.

The $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ hydrolysis of a tertiary halide is the classic case: two species in the equation, one in the rate law, because the slow step is ionisation alone.

questions.q: State Le Chatelier's principle and apply it to the Contact process, $2\text{SO}_{2} + \text{O}_{2} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{SO}_{3}$ ($\Delta H = -196$ kJ/mol), explaining the conditions actually used.
questions.solution:
**The principle.** If a change is imposed on a system at equilibrium, the position of equilibrium shifts so as to **oppose** that change.

**Applying it.**

**Temperature.** The forward reaction is exothermic, so **lowering** the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right and raises $K$ — a higher yield.

**Pressure.** There are 3 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right, so **high pressure** shifts equilibrium to the right.

**Concentration.** An **excess of air** (cheap and plentiful) pushes the equilibrium right.

**The conditions actually used: about $450$°C, only $1$–$2$ atm, and a $\text{V}_{2}\text{O}_{5}$ catalyst.**

**Why not a lower temperature?** The yield would be higher but the **rate** would be hopelessly slow. $450$°C is a **compromise** between yield and speed, and the catalyst is what makes that compromise affordable.

**Why not high pressure, when the theory calls for it?** Because the yield is already about $96\%$ at atmospheric pressure. The extra few per cent would not repay the enormous cost of pressure vessels and compressors.

That is the practical lesson of this example, and the contrast with the Haber process — where the equilibrium is far less favourable, so $200$ atm **is** worth paying for.

**The catalyst's role,** in both processes, is to reach equilibrium quickly. It never changes where that equilibrium lies.

questions.q: Write the expression for $K_{c}$ for $\text{N}_{2} + 3\text{H}_{2} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_{3}$, explain what the magnitude tells you, and calculate $K_{c}$ given equilibrium concentrations of $0.2$, $0.6$ and $0.4$ mol dm$^{-3}$ respectively.
questions.solution:
**The expression.** Products over reactants, each raised to the power of its coefficient:

$K_{c} = \dfrac{[\text{NH}_{3}]^{2}}{[\text{N}_{2}][\text{H}_{2}]^{3}}$

**What the magnitude means.**

• $K_{c} \gg 1$ — the equilibrium lies well to the **right**; the reaction is nearly complete.

• $K_{c} \ll 1$ — it lies to the **left**; very little product forms.

• $K_{c} \approx 1$ — appreciable amounts of everything are present.

**It says nothing whatever about rate.** A reaction may have an enormous $K_{c}$ and still be immeasurably slow — the conversion of diamond to graphite, for instance.

**The calculation.**

$K_{c} = \dfrac{(0.4)^{2}}{(0.2)(0.6)^{3}} = \dfrac{0.16}{0.2 \times 0.216} = \dfrac{0.16}{0.0432} = \mathbf{3.70}$

**Units.** $K_{c}$ has units $\dfrac{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^{2}}{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^{4}} = \text{mol}^{-2}\text{dm}^{6}$ — they must be worked out from the expression each time, and only cancel when the moles of gas are equal on both sides.

**What changes $K_{c}$.** Only **temperature**. Adding more nitrogen shifts the position of equilibrium but the system adjusts until the same ratio is restored — which is exactly what makes $K_{c}$ a **constant**.

questions.topic: Collision theory and the Boltzmann distribution
questions.q: Use the Boltzmann distribution to explain why a small temperature rise increases the rate so dramatically, and why a catalyst does the same.
questions.solution:
**The Boltzmann distribution** shows how molecular energies are spread at a given temperature: it starts at the origin, rises to a peak, and has a long tail to the right.

Only molecules in that tail, with energy exceeding $E_{a}$, can react on collision.

**Raising the temperature.** The curve flattens and **shifts right**: the peak lowers and moves to higher energy, and the tail extends.

The total area is unchanged — the number of molecules is fixed — but the **area beyond $E_{a}$ increases sharply**.

**Why the effect is so large.** The tail falls off **exponentially**, as $e^{-E_{a}/RT}$, so even a small shift multiplies the number of molecules beyond the barrier.

A $10$ K rise near room temperature typically **doubles** the rate.

**The common misconception** is that this is because collisions are more frequent. The collision frequency rises only a few per cent for a $10$ K rise — nothing like enough. It is almost entirely the **energy distribution** that matters.

**A catalyst** works on the same diagram from the other direction. The distribution is **unchanged**, but $E_{a}$ moves **left** to a lower value.

A far larger area of the same curve now lies beyond it, so many more collisions succeed.

**One curve, two ways of getting more molecules over the barrier:** move the molecules, or move the barrier.

questions.q: Explain what a rate-determining step is, and show how the rate equation gives evidence about the mechanism of the hydrolysis of a tertiary halogenoalkane.
questions.solution:
**The rate-determining step** is the **slowest** step in a multi-step mechanism. The whole reaction can go no faster than its slowest stage.

**Only species involved up to and including that step appear in the rate equation** — which is why the rate law so often disagrees with the balanced equation, and why that disagreement is informative.

**The tertiary halide.** For

$(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CBr} + \text{OH}^{-} \to (\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{COH} + \text{Br}^{-}$

the experimental rate equation is

$\text{rate} = k\left[(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CBr}\right]$

**The hydroxide does not appear at all** — the rate is unchanged if its concentration is doubled.

**What that proves.** The slow step must involve the halide **alone**:

**Step 1 (slow):** $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CBr} \to (\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{C}^{+} + \text{Br}^{-}$

**Step 2 (fast):** $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{C}^{+} + \text{OH}^{-} \to (\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{COH}$

This is the $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ mechanism, and the carbocation is stabilised by the three electron-releasing methyl groups.

**Contrast a primary halide**, where the rate equation is

$\text{rate} = k[\text{RBr}][\text{OH}^{-}]$

— second order, because both species are in the single slow step. That is $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$, and there is no carbocation at all.

**The stereochemistry confirms both.** $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ goes through a planar cation and gives a racemic product; $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ inverts the configuration. Kinetics and stereochemistry agree, which is what makes the mechanisms believable.
